title: Who makes the rules for AI?
essentialQuestion: Who should decide how AI is used, and what rules make it fair?
learningGoal: Compare how different groups make rules for AI, and recommend how a use of AI should be handled, kept separate from what one law says.

warmUp.question: Who do you think should make rules for AI?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: What does each person want? Whose voice might be missing?

cards.title: A town meeting in Hillford about AI
rows: “A camera that knows every face in the market could catch thieves.”
“If an AI tool marks our tests, we want a person to check it. We want a say in the rules.”
“A tool could help us see who needs help first. But a nurse must always check it.”
“Some of us don't use phones. Don't make AI the only way to get help from the council.”
“A chatbot could answer questions at night. It should say clearly that it is a machine.”
A resident who moved to Hillford last year
“I can't vote here yet, but I use the council's services too. Ask people like me.”

activity.title: Help the Hillford council
activity.instructions: The Hillford council has ideas for using AI. Put each idea in the group you would recommend. There is no score, and more than one answer can make sense. After you place one, you see one possible answer and a reason. Then, as a separate point, you see what the European Union (EU) AI law says.

items.text: A tool gives every person a “good citizen” score. The score decides who gets help.
items.feedback: A score like this can be unfair to whole groups. In the EU, the law bans scores like this.

items.text: A camera in class reads students' faces to guess how they feel.
items.feedback: Feelings are private, and guesses can be wrong. Some say it could spot a student who needs help. In the EU, the law bans this in schools, except for health or safety.

items.text: Police cameras in the market recognise every face, live, all day.
items.feedback: It watches everyone, all day. Others say it could catch thieves, so people disagree. In the EU, the law bans this for police, except in a few serious cases, like finding a missing person.
A wrong mark could change a student's future, so a person should check. In the EU, the law calls this high risk. Its strict rules for it start in December 2027.

items.text: A tool helps the clinic see which patients need help first.
items.feedback: A mistake could harm someone's health, so a nurse or doctor should check. In the EU, the law counts many health tools as high risk.

items.text: A tool sorts reports about broken street lights. It sends each one to the right team.
items.feedback: It can help reports reach the right team faster, and people still fix the lights. A real tool like this works in Thailand. Strict rules could make sense too, if it decides whose problem comes first.

items.text: A chatbot on the council's website answers questions about bus times.
items.feedback: It helps people at night, if they know it is a machine. In the EU, the law says people must be told it is a machine.

items.text: A filter stops junk messages from reaching the council.
items.feedback: It is low risk and saves time. In the EU, the AI law has no special rules for it. But other laws, like privacy laws, still apply.

items.text: A game at the library uses AI to move its characters.
items.feedback: It is low risk and just for fun. In the EU, the AI law has no special rules for games like this.

activity.saves: The group the learner chose for each idea, with the lesson's other answers.
activity.offline: Everything is in the lesson file. Nothing is sent anywhere.

sections.heading: Many groups make rules for AI
sections.text: New technology brings questions about who it helps, who it might harm and who decides. In the made-up town of Hillford, the council wants to use AI, so it holds a meeting first. A shop owner, students, a nurse, an older neighbour and a newer resident who can't vote all give their views. In the real world, many groups make rules for AI. Governments make laws, which everyone must follow. Companies write rules for their own tools. Groups of countries agree on a guideline, which is advice that countries can choose to use. Residents, including young people, can share their ideas too.
sections.simpler: Who does a new tool help or harm? Who decides? In made-up Hillford, the council holds a meeting about AI. Many residents share their views, even some who can't vote. Governments make laws. Everyone must follow a law. Companies make rules for their tools. Groups of countries agree on a guideline. A guideline is advice. Young people can share ideas too.

sections.heading: Guidelines, a law and levels of risk
sections.text: In 2021, all 193 member states of UNESCO adopted the first global agreement on the ethics of AI, which says AI should protect human rights and stay under human control. In 2024, the countries of ASEAN in Southeast Asia shared a guide for AI, with ideas such as fairness, privacy and safety. Both are guidelines. The European Union (EU) made a law that came into force in August 2024, with parts starting on different dates. It sorts uses of AI by risk, which means how much harm they could do. Some uses are banned, such as scores that treat people unfairly. Some are high risk, such as marking exams, so they need strict checks. Most uses, like spam filters, have no special AI rules, but other laws, like privacy laws, still apply.
sections.simpler: In 2021, 193 countries agreed on ideas for AI at UNESCO. AI should protect human rights. People should stay in control. In 2024, countries in Southeast Asia shared a guide for AI. These are guidelines. The European Union (EU) made a law in 2024. Its parts start at different times. It sorts AI by risk. Risk means how much harm it could do. Some uses are banned, like unfair scores. Some are high risk, like marking exams. Most uses have no special AI rules. But other laws, like privacy laws, still apply.

sections.heading: A real service, and your own view
sections.text: In Thailand, people report problems such as broken roads, floods or street lights on Traffy Fondue, a public platform built by a national science agency. Its AI sorts each report and sends it to the right office, where people still decide what to do and fix it. Its makers say it received over 940,000 reports in two years. That shows many people use it, not how well each problem was solved. What a law says is one answer. Your own recommendation can be different, if you give reasons.
sections.simpler: In Thailand, people report problems like broken roads on Traffy Fondue, a public tool. Its AI sorts each report and sends it to the right office. People there still fix the problem. Its makers say it got over 940,000 reports in two years. That shows people use it, not how well problems were fixed. What a law says is one answer. Your view can be different, with reasons.

glossary.definition: A rule made by a government that everyone must follow.
glossary.example: The European Union's AI law bans some uses of AI.

glossary.definition: Advice about how to do something. People can choose to follow it.
glossary.example: The guide from countries in Southeast Asia is a guideline, not a law.

glossary.definition: A person who lives in a place.
glossary.example: Every resident of Hillford was asked to the meeting, even those who can't vote.

glossary.definition: The chance that something bad could happen.
glossary.example: A tool that marks exams is high risk.

glossary.definition: Things every person should have or be free to do.
glossary.example: Privacy is one of the rights that rules for AI protect.

checks.question: How does the European Union's AI law sort uses of AI?

options.feedback: Not quite. The age of a tool is not what counts. Read the second section.
Not quite. The same rules apply to every company. Read the second section.

options.text: By how much harm it could do
options.feedback: Yes. The law sorts AI by risk. Uses that could do the most harm are banned.

checks.question: A spam filter has no special rules under the European Union's AI law. What does that mean?

options.text: No laws at all apply to it
options.feedback: Not quite. Other laws, like privacy laws, still apply. Read the second section.

options.text: Other laws, like privacy laws, still apply
options.feedback: Yes. No special AI rules does not mean no rules at all.

options.text: It is banned everywhere in the European Union
options.feedback: Not quite. Banned uses are things like unfair scores. Read the second section.

write.prompt: Choose one Hillford idea for AI. Say what you recommend, and why. Then, as a separate point, say what the EU law says and whose views the council should hear.

The council should listen to ___, because ...
selfCheck: I gave my recommendation and a reason.
I said what the law says, as a separate point.
I said whose views the council should hear.
write.example: I chose the tool that marks exams. I recommend allowing it with strict rules, because a wrong mark could change a student's future. A teacher should check every mark. Someone could disagree, because the tool saves time. As a separate point, the EU law says marking exams is high risk, so it needs strict checks. The council should listen to students, because the tool affects them most.

watch.title: Ethics of AI: Challenges and Governance
watch.why: UNESCO, which made the global agreement in this lesson, looks at how different parts of the world are making rules for AI.
watch.beforeQuestion: What do you think a fair rule for AI would protect?
watch.afterQuestion: Why is it hard to turn good ideas about AI into real rules?
watch.summary: This video is from UNESCO. UNESCO is a world group that works on schools, science and culture. The video is part of a series about the ethics of AI. Ethics means what is right and wrong. The video asks a big question. How can people get the good things from AI without making gaps between people bigger? AI could also bring new kinds of unfair results. The video says people around the world seem to agree on some ideas. These include privacy, equal treatment and leaving no one out. The hard part is turning these ideas into real rules. The video looks at how different parts of the world are making rules for AI. It also asks what would make rules fair for everyone, everywhere.
keyPoints: Many people agree on some ideas for AI, such as privacy, equal treatment and leaving no one out.
The hard part is turning these ideas into real rules.
Different parts of the world are making different rules for AI.
watch.contentNote: About 7 minutes (412 seconds, from YouTube's listing), adult level, from February 2023, before the European Union's AI law was agreed, so it may describe that law as a plan. UNESCO's description says subtitles are available in English, French, Japanese and other languages. The title and channel were confirmed with YouTube's oEmbed on 31 October 2026. The summary was written from UNESCO's own description of the video, not from watching it. Someone on the team must watch it before learners use it; learners can read the written summary instead.

visual.description: PLACEHOLDER: no picture exists yet, and visuals/DW16.svg is only a planned path. A pyramid in four layers, with a word label and a simple symbol on each, titled “One example: the European Union's AI law”. Top (smallest): “Banned” with a crossed-out circle, and two small examples: “Unfair scores for how people behave” and “Guessing students' feelings”. Second: “Strict rules” with a magnifying glass, example “Marking exams”. Third: “Must say it is AI” with a speech bubble, example “Chatbots”. Bottom (widest): “No special AI rules (other laws still apply)” with a tick, examples “Spam filters” and “Games”. Beside the pyramid, a small group of simple drawn people labelled “Who decides? Governments, companies, groups of countries, residents”. Words carry every meaning, so colour is never the only clue.
visual.alt: One example, the European Union's AI law, as a pyramid of risk levels: banned uses at the top, then uses with strict rules, then uses that must say they are AI, and most uses with no special AI rules at the bottom, where other laws still apply.

sensitiveNotes: Rules about cameras, scores and surveillance can be close to home for learners who have lived under heavy policing, in camps or at borders. Keep the discussion on made-up Hillford. Never ask learners about the laws, police or government of any country they have lived in, or how they were checked or recorded; let them speak only if they choose to.
educatorNotes: Keep two questions apart: “What do you recommend for Hillford?” (the learner's view, marked on reasons) and “What does the European Union's law say?” (a fact about one jurisdiction). Never mark a recommendation wrong because it differs from the EU law. The AI Act (in force 1 August 2024) bans, from 2 February 2025, social scoring that leads to unjustified or unrelated harmful treatment, emotion recognition in workplaces and schools except for medical or safety reasons, and live face identification by police in public places except for three narrow purposes (searching for victims or missing persons, preventing an imminent threat, and finding suspects of serious crimes). Transparency rules (chatbots, labelled deepfakes) apply from August 2026. After the AI Omnibus (in force 27 July 2026), high-risk rules for uses such as exam scoring apply from 2 December 2027, and for AI in regulated products from 2 August 2028; check the Commission's page before quoting dates. Minimal-risk uses (spam filters, games) have no AI Act rules, but data protection, consumer protection and product safety law still apply (Article 2). The market-camera item is about police; a council's or shop's face cameras would fall under other rules. Paper version: the nine ideas on cards under three headings.

Traffy Fondue (Thailand) was developed by NECTEC, part of the National Science and Technology Development Agency (NSTDA). Residents report through a LINE chatbot with a location and photo; since 2024 its AI also summarises reports, ranks them by urgency, suggests fixes and filters rude words, as well as classifying them and sending each to the responsible agency. NSTDA reports more than 940,000 reports from June 2022 to July 2024, over 733,000 of them “completed” (77%), across 77 provinces and more than 15,000 agencies. These are the operator's own figures: completed is a status in the system, not an independent check of repairs. It is an operating service, not a measured impact.

To localise: Indonesia's Minister of Communication and Informatics issued a circular on AI ethics (Surat Edaran No. 9 of 2023), and Malaysia launched voluntary national guidelines in 2024 (link in the claim record, content/courses/digital-world/claims/DW16.md). Like the UNESCO and ASEAN texts, both are guidance rather than laws. Present every approach neutrally; the lesson compares, it doesn't rank countries.

Revised on 1 November 2026 from Justin's review: the activity, Write task, starters, self-check and example now keep “What do you recommend?” apart from “What does the European Union's law say?”; feedback gives a reason, says when people disagree, and gives the EU rule as a separate point, never as the right answer. EU facts checked against the Commission's page and the Act's text (1 November 2026): exceptions added (emotion recognition for medical or safety reasons; police face identification in a few serious cases, so the market-camera item now says police), high-risk dates after the AI Omnibus (December 2027), and “no special AI rules” now says other laws, such as privacy laws, still apply (new quick check). A real Southeast Asian public service, Traffy Fondue (Thailand), is in the reading, with a new sort item: AI sorts and routes residents' reports, people still respond, and a report count is not problems solved. Residents replace citizens (glossary, warm-up, visual), and a made-up resident who can't vote joins the Hillford meeting. The Hillford evidence stays fully fictional; the real case is in the reading, the teacher notes and sources. To stay within six sources, the 2020 White Paper consultation (its sentence was cut) and Malaysia's guidelines page were dropped (Malaysia's link is in the claim record).
